(i) thiamine deficiency results in neuronal death in selective brain regions, (ii) the pathogenesis of thiamine deficiency is complex and involves multiple mechanisms, (iii) non-invasive imaging techniques such as MRI and CT are of limited use in the assessment of brain pathology in WE and (iv) PET imaging of astroglial markers may provide an accurate assessment of brain damage due to WE.

the elucidation of the pathophysiology of neuronal loss in WE, and the potential use of PET imaging techniques in the assessment of this disorder in man.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pathogenesis of brain damage in thiamine-deficit is multifactorial, and that the neuronal loss may not be a direct consequence of thiamine deficiency, but rather secondary to the effects of other factors.

the mechanisms involved in neuronal death in WE include, (i) a direct toxic action of the pyrithiamin, (ii) impaired energy metabolism, (iii) excitatory amino acid toxicity and (iv) a role of astrocytes in the pathogenesis.

thiamine deficiency results in selective neuronal loss in the brain.

the pathophysiologic mechanism of neuronal cell death in WE may involve NMDA-receptors and the blood-brain barrier, and that PET ligands for these mechanisms may offer useful diagnostic tools for the evaluation of WE in humans.
the pathophysiological mechanisms of thiamine deficiency in the rat closely mimic those in humans, and that 11C-PK-11195 is an ideal PET ligand for imaging the brain lesions in WE.

the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying neuronal cell death in thiamine-deficit are not fully understood.
